extracted.intended_audience: Authors (especially mathematics education researchers and early-career researchers) preparing submissions for the journal Mathematical Thinking and Learning and similar mathematics-education journals
extracted.subtask_short: submitting to Mathematical Thinking and Learning
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for preparing and revising manuscripts for submission to the journal Mathematical Thinking and Learning (MTL), covering scope, manuscript components (title, abstract, literature review, methods, results, discussion), formatting, and responding to peer review. Emphasis on maximizing chances of acceptance and avoiding common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit to journal aims and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the submission meets the aims and scope of Mathematical Thinking and Learning (MTL): articles primarily addressing mathematical thinking, reasoning, and learning, potentially interdisciplinary (psychology, sociology, philosophy, anthropology, IT), including empirical, theoretical/philosophical analyses, Short Reports, book reviews, and occasional special issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether your topic (e.g., interdisciplinary studies, technological impacts, processes of mathematical reasoning, development across lifespan, changing perspectives on mathematics, cross-cultural studies, innovative instructional practices) matches MTL. Submissions that do not meet aims/scope are often rejected outright; if out of scope, consider alternative journals (e.g., educational psychology outlets). Read a range of articles in the journal to understand its nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate article type and length (Short Reports etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the correct article type: full research article, Short Report (~around 15 manuscript pages), theoretical/philosophical analysis, discourse pieces, letters to the editor, or critical commentaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short Reports may document pilot or introductory studies, proposals for further research, or timely theoretical pieces; they typically comprise around 15 manuscript pages. Match content and length to the article type and journal expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow journal style guidelines (APA 6th edition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere strictly to MTL/Taylor & Francis style guidelines, including APA (6th ed.) conventions for layout, referencing, spelling (Merriam-Webster), section headings, line spacing, font type, table/figure requirements, and word/page limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors will often return submissions prior to external review if these guidelines are not followed (especially page/word limits). Check MTL author instructions on the journal website and apply APA formatting consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, concise, and appropriate title
rubrics_metrics.description: Article titles must be clear, concise, accurately represent contents, suitable for electronic indexing, and not overly long or more appropriate for professional (non-research) journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid very long titles and titles that mislead indexing. A title that is off-putting can negatively influence initial editorial impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informative abstract (150–250 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts should, within ~150–250 words (depending on journal), convey the study's purpose, methodology, key findings, and conclusions/implications, and include keywords for indexing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a 'complete but concise description' so reviewers are 'captured' and motivated to read the paper. State 1–2 key findings, 1–2 central assertions about why findings occurred, and 1–2 conclusions/implications. Poorly written abstracts create poor first impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature review: critical, current, gap-focused
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature reviews should go beyond reporting to critically analyse existing work, highlight gaps, indicate the significance of the problem, and show how the study advances the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid brevity, omission of key studies, dated or irrelevant literature, country-confined literature for international journals, and failure to state the problem clearly. Use the review to build the theoretical/conceptual framework and justify the study's contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical/conceptual framework presence and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a coherent theoretical or conceptual framework that guides research questions, data collection, analysis, and discussion, and shows how the study emanates from conceptual foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frameworks should potentially advance the field; lack of framing often reduces impact. If parts of the framework were published elsewhere, clearly indicate the unique contribution of the current article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological detail: participants and sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the nature, number, and background of participants, the population they were drawn from, and how they were chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers must be able to judge validity; omission makes validity claims difficult to evaluate. Include enough detail to allow interpretation and potential replication where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological detail: instruments and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe instruments developed or used, how they were administered, their appropriateness for the research questions, their reliability, and provide samples of items or the full instrument where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include examples or appendices for questionnaires/tests. Failure to include instrument details undermines confidence in results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match between claimed methodology and actual procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the described research approach (e.g., 'teaching experiment') actually fits the methodology used and is supported by appropriate citations and explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers check for consistency between claimed method philosophy and procedures; mismatches (claiming an approach but not following it) lead to criticism and possible rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of variables for causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For experimental studies, control variables appropriately if causal inferences are to be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers will look for potential confounding factors and competing hypotheses. Clearly describe controls, randomization, and procedures to support causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent justification and reporting of data analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Data analysis procedures should be precisely and transparently described from the beginning through presentation of outcomes, making clear how analyses address research questions and lead to reported outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow AERA guidance: make the relevance of analysis procedures to problem formulation explicit. Justify choice of analytic techniques and show stepwise how they answer the research questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and organise results to address research questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Organise results with the research questions in mind, revisiting each question in turn and reporting only those results that answer them; unexpected findings belong in the discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reporting results that address other issues; structure results so they directly map to questions. Use unanticipated outcomes in discussion as grounds for further research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claims and conclusions with data
rubrics_metrics.description: All claims and conclusions must be supported by the data; avoid generalisations not backed by evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use triangulation, independent coding, and critical reflection on researchers' pre-existing perspectives. Provide concrete participant examples (e.g., excerpts from classroom discussions) to substantiate claims like metacognitive activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of tables and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tables/figures only when they clarify or summarise outcomes involving multiple data points; fewer tables are generally better and must be interpretable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarise table/figure messages in the text. Ensure legibility (font size), avoid overly dense figures, and be cautious with colour (printed issues incur colour costs; use shading as substitute where necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: In-depth, interpretive discussion linked to framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion should summarise outcomes and provide an interpretive commentary explaining how each research question was addressed, reasons for outcomes, contextual factors, links to or challenges of existing theory, and alternative interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect outcomes back to the theoretical framework, indicate how findings support or challenge theory, and discuss implications (theoretical, practical, methodological) only insofar as they are justified by the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit claims and recommendations to what the data support
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit discussion/conclusions and recommendations to what is warranted by the study's data; avoid overreaching into broad educational policy or practice recommendations not supported by evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robinson et al. suggest restricting recommendations for practice in primary educational research journals to maintain separation between evidence and opinion. Maintain clear distinction between evidence-based implications and opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate contribution to the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly indicate how the study extends current work in the field and argues the nature of its contribution (not merely reinforcing well-established research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the study duplicates prior findings, argue the nature of the contribution (e.g., context variation, replication effects) and suggest implications for further studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limitations and suggest remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge the study's limitations (sample size, methods, etc.) and recommend ways these limitations could be reduced in future work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include limitations in the discussion or a separate section; suggest practical remedies (e.g., larger sample, interviews for deeper insights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions: succinct summary and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a brief concluding section that states key outcomes, justifies their significance with reference to related studies, and offers core conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions should be brief and may include recommendations for future research. Avoid repeating lengthy discussion material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference accuracy and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure all in-text citations appear in the reference list and vice versa; references must be correctly formatted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrectly listed references waste reviewers' time and undermine credibility. Use APA 6th ed. format as required by MTL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript structure and readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the submission in recommended order (title page, abstract, text, quotations, acknowledgments, references, appendices, footnotes, tables and figures), ensure cohesion, readability, and freedom from typographical errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reader-friendly, well-flowing manuscript is essential. Non-native English authors should seek editorial assistance. Poor readability may cause editors/reviewers to decline review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission formatting and blinding
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow submission formatting requirements: blinded submissions (avoid self-identifying material), non-numbered section headings as required, double line spacing, separate figure/table files when requested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-blinded submissions are a common mistake and may concern reviewers. Check and follow specific formatting instructions on the MTL submission page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of appendices and supplementary material
rubrics_metrics.description: Include lengthy or distracting materials (e.g., questionnaires, tests, full instruments) as appendices or supplementary electronic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APA provides instructions on appendices. Appendices help keep the main text readable while providing full methodological detail for interested readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand peer-review process and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect rigorous, double-blind peer review by at least three reviewers after editorial screening, with reviewers typically allowed up to six weeks and common delays due to reviewer decline/late submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions commonly request revisions rather than immediate acceptance; multiple rounds of revision are not uncommon. Editors may seek advice from associate editors for borderline papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare thorough, specific responses to reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: When revising, respond to reviewers' feedback in a detailed, specific, and easy-to-follow manner; describe revisions made and why some suggestions were not followed where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague responses ('manuscript is now much improved') are insufficient. Consider presenting responses in table format. Explain explicitly where changes were made (page/line) and why any suggested change was not adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of international scope in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: MTL is an international journal; authors should not confine citations to research or curriculum from their own country but consider relevant international literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite cross-national studies and international perspectives where appropriate to situate work in the broader field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for early-career researchers and reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions from beginning researchers are welcomed; the journal offers support and encourages young researchers (including competent doctoral students) to undertake reviews under supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early-career authors should seek mentorship and editorial assistance; junior reviewers may contribute useful reviews under advisor guidance.
